lessons.title: A Warm No
lessons.summary: You can turn something down and still sound caring.

steps.title: Warmth plus a clear no
steps.body: A kind no has two parts: something warm about the person, and a clear answer. “I’m so glad you asked me, and I can’t make it” respects both of you.

steps.prompt: A friend invites you to a party on the one night you’d planned to rest. What’s a warm, clear no?

options.text: “Maybe! I’ll see how I feel.”
options.why: A vague maybe keeps them waiting and leaves you feeling obliged.

options.text: “Thank you for inviting me! I need a quiet night, but have a brilliant time.”
options.why: It thanks them, gives a clear answer and wishes them well.

options.text: “Parties aren’t really my thing.”
options.why: It’s honest, but it can sound like you’re dismissing them and their plans.

steps.prompt: Add warmth to your no.
steps.before: I really appreciate you thinking of me,
steps.why: “And I’ll pass” keeps the warmth and the no together, without sounding grudging.

steps.prompt: Who do you find it hardest to say no to?
steps.reply: Good to know. Practising a warm no with them could make a big difference to your energy.

steps.body: The next time you need to say no, start with one warm sentence, then give your clear answer.

lessons.title: No Without the Essay
lessons.summary: You don’t owe a long list of reasons for every no.

steps.title: Over-explaining invites debate
steps.body: Long excuses can make a no sound negotiable: people start solving your reasons. A short, kind answer is often clearer and easier for everyone.

steps.prompt: Short and clear, or an essay?

cards.text: “I would, but my cousin might visit and I’ve got washing and…”
“Well, I could maybe move things if you really needed…”

steps.why: Short answers are clear and final. Essays give people things to argue with, which makes your no feel shaky.

steps.title: A favour you can’t do

lines.text: Could you feed my cats all next week? 🐱

steps.prompt: You can’t this time. What do you send?

options.text: I can’t next week, sorry! Hope you find someone 🐾
options.why: Kind, clear and short, with no reasons for them to try and work around.

options.text: Well, I’ve got a busy week and maybe a trip and work stuff, so possibly not…
options.reaction: So… is that a yes on the quiet days?
options.why: The long list makes it sound like a maybe they can negotiate.

options.text: Ignore it and hope they ask someone else.
options.why: Silence leaves them stuck and makes things awkward later.

steps.prompt: Why do you explain your no so much?
steps.reply: Those are kind reasons. A warm tone does the job just as well as a long explanation.

steps.body: Say your next no in one or two sentences, with no more than one short reason.

lessons.title: Offer What You Can
lessons.summary: A “no, but” can protect your limits and still help.

steps.title: The middle option
steps.body: Sometimes the answer isn’t yes or no but “not that, but this”. Offering what you can genuinely give keeps your limit and shows you still care.

steps.prompt: Match the request to a “no, but” offer.

pairs.a: “Can you help me move all day?”
pairs.b: “I can do two hours in the morning.”
“I can’t, but I’ll help you budget.”
“Not this year, but I’ll bring dessert.”

steps.why: Each offer is honest about your limit and still gives something real, so the relationship feels supported.

steps.prompt: Your friend asks you to babysit every Friday. You can’t commit to that. What’s best?

options.text: Say yes and hope you can keep it up.
options.why: Agreeing to more than you can give often ends in resentment or letting them down.

options.text: Say no and leave it there.
options.why: That’s okay, but you may be missing a chance to help in a way that suits you.

options.text: “Every week is too much for me, but I could do one Friday a month.”
options.why: It’s honest about your limit and offers real, sustainable help.

steps.prompt: Offer the middle option.
steps.before: I can’t do the whole day,
words: but I could do the afternoon.
steps.answer: but I could do the afternoon.
steps.why: It keeps your limit clear while still offering something genuinely helpful.

steps.body: Next time you’re asked for more than you can give, offer a smaller version that genuinely works for you.

lessons.title: Protect Your Rest
lessons.summary: Rest is a real plan, not just empty time.

steps.title: Rest counts as a plan
steps.body: If your quiet evening is easy to give away, it will be. Treating rest as a real commitment, like any other plan, helps you protect it without guilt.

steps.prompt: You’ve kept Sunday free to recharge. A friend asks you to help with a car-boot sale. What’s best?

options.text: “Sunday’s my rest day, but I could help price things on Saturday evening.”
options.why: You protect your rest and still offer help at a time that works.

options.text: Say yes because resting isn’t a real reason.
options.why: Rest is a real need. Giving it up often leaves you worn out all week.

options.text: “I’ve got plans.” and feel guilty all day.
options.why: Fine to say, but rest doesn’t need guilt attached.

steps.prompt: Protects rest, or chips away at it?

cards.text: Saying yes to every weekend plan

steps.why: Protected rest refills your energy for the people you love. Without it, you have less to give everyone.

steps.prompt: What usually steals your rest time?
steps.reply: Naming the thief is the first step to guarding your rest from it.

steps.body: Block out one rest slot in your calendar this week and treat it like any other plan.

lessons.title: Spot the Overbooking
lessons.summary: Check your energy before saying yes, not after.

steps.title: Yes now, regret later
steps.body: Saying yes is easy in the moment. The cost arrives later, when the week is full and you’re exhausted. A quick pause to check your diary and energy prevents that.

steps.prompt: Put a healthy yes-or-no check in order.
steps.why: Pausing gives you room to think. Checking both time and energy helps you only agree to what you can truly enjoy.

steps.prompt: Buy yourself a moment.
steps.why: It’s friendly and gives you time to check if you really have the room.

steps.prompt: Your week already has four evening plans. Someone invites you to a fifth. What’s wise?

options.text: Squeeze it in; you can sleep at the weekend.
options.why: Running on empty all week usually catches up with you.

options.text: “I’d love to, but this week is full. Next week?”
options.why: You protect your energy and keep the door open.

options.text: Say yes, then cancel on the day.
options.why: Late cancelling can hurt more than an honest no up front.

steps.body: Before agreeing to anything new this week, check both your diary and your energy first.

lessons.title: Ask for Help Sooner
lessons.summary: Saying “I can’t do it all” is a boundary too.

steps.title: Doing it all isn’t a badge
steps.body: Carrying everything alone often looks strong but leads to burnout. Saying “I need some help with this” is a healthy limit, not a failure.

steps.title: Too much on your plate

lines.text: You okay? You seem really frazzled.
Is there anything I can do?

steps.prompt: You’re overwhelmed. What do you say?

options.text: I’m fine, I’ll manage.
options.why: Turning down a genuine offer leaves you carrying everything alone.

options.text: Yes please! Could you take over dinner tonight?
options.why: Accepting with a specific ask lightens your load and lets them help in a clear way.

options.text: You never help anyway.
options.reaction: That’s not fair, I’m offering now…
options.why: Old frustration shuts down the help being offered right now.

steps.prompt: Match the overload to a clear ask.
steps.why: Specific asks are easy to say yes to, and they share the load before you burn out.

steps.prompt: What stops you asking for help?
steps.reply: All understandable. Most people feel glad to be asked for something specific.

steps.body: Ask someone for help with one specific task this week, before you reach the point of feeling overwhelmed.

lessons.title: Reply When You Can
lessons.summary: You don’t have to answer every message straight away.

steps.title: Instant replies aren’t a rule
steps.body: Phones make it feel like every message needs an answer right now. It doesn’t. Replying when you have the time and energy is a healthy, normal limit.

steps.prompt: A friend sends a long message while you’re at dinner with family. What’s healthy?

options.text: Reply properly later when you have time.
options.why: They get a thoughtful answer, and you stay present with your family.

options.text: Stop eating and reply in full straight away.
options.why: You lose the moment you’re in, and a rushed reply may not be your best.

options.text: Leave it for a week without saying anything.
options.why: A very long silence can leave them worried or hurt.

steps.prompt: Set a kind expectation.
steps.why: A quick holding reply lets them know you care and when to expect more.

steps.prompt: How do you feel when you haven’t replied to a message?
steps.reply: If guilt creeps in, a quick “Will reply later!” can ease it without losing your time.

steps.body: Next time you get a message at a busy moment, send a short holding reply and answer properly later.

lessons.title: Phone-Free Moments
lessons.summary: Agree on times when screens go away.

steps.title: Screens steal moments
steps.body: Meals, walks and bedtime are some of the best chances to connect. Agreeing together on a few phone-free times can make them feel special again.

steps.prompt: Good phone-free moment, or not needed?

cards.text: The first ten minutes after getting home

steps.why: Phone-free moments protect time for each other. Phones aren’t the enemy, they just shouldn’t crowd out connection.

steps.prompt: You’d like dinners to be phone-free at home. What’s the best way to suggest it?

options.text: Take everyone’s phones away at the table.
options.why: Enforcing it suddenly can feel controlling and cause a backlash.

options.text: “Could we try phone-free dinners this week and see how it feels?”
options.why: A friendly trial invites everyone in rather than imposing a rule.

options.text: Sigh loudly whenever someone looks at their phone.
options.why: Hinting by sighing tends to annoy people without changing anything.

steps.prompt: When would a phone-free moment help you most?
steps.reply: Great pick. Start there for a week and see what changes.

steps.body: Suggest one phone-free moment to the people you live with, and try it together for a week.

lessons.title: Agree on Sharing Online
lessons.summary: Talk about what’s okay to post about each other.

steps.title: Everyone’s comfort differs
steps.body: Some people love sharing their life online; others prefer to keep things private. Agreeing what’s okay to post about each other avoids hurt and surprises.

steps.title: A photo dilemma

lines.text: Just posted the pics from last night! 📸

steps.prompt: You’d rather not be in public posts. What do you say?

options.text: Delete them now!!
options.why: Your limit is fair, but a sharp demand can feel like an attack.

options.text: Say nothing and feel uncomfortable.
options.why: Without telling them, they can’t know your preference.

options.text: Thank you! I’m quite private online though. Could you take down the ones with me in?
options.reaction: Oh, of course! Didn’t know, done now 😊
options.why: Kind and clear, it explains your preference and asks for one simple change.

steps.prompt: Match the situation to a clear agreement.
steps.why: Agreements made calmly in advance save hurt feelings later and help everyone feel respected.

steps.prompt: How private are you online?
steps.reply: Knowing your own comfort level makes it much easier to explain it to others.

steps.body: Have a quick, relaxed chat with someone close about what you’re both happy to share about each other online.

lessons.title: Care Without Carrying
lessons.summary: You can support someone without taking on all their feelings.

steps.title: Support isn’t absorbing
steps.body: Caring deeply can mean carrying someone’s worries as if they were your own. You can listen and support them while still remembering their feelings belong to them.

steps.prompt: Healthy support, or carrying too much?

cards.text: Listening, then going to bed on time
Lying awake worrying about their problem every night
Feeling it’s your job to make them happy

steps.why: Healthy support stays kind without draining you. Carrying too much can leave you exhausted and less able to help.

steps.prompt: Your friend calls every night to talk through the same worry. You’re wiped out. What’s healthy?

options.text: Keep taking every call, however late.
options.why: Running on empty helps neither of you in the long run.

options.text: Stop answering without explaining.
options.why: Disappearing suddenly can feel like abandonment.

options.text: “I care about you. Could we talk on Sundays, and could you lean on others too?”
options.why: It keeps your support while setting a limit and pointing them to more help.

steps.prompt: Whose feelings do you tend to carry most?
steps.reply: That shows how much you care. Remember, you can care deeply without carrying it all.

steps.body: After supporting someone today, do one small thing to set their worry down and look after yourself.

lessons.title: Not Your Job to Fix
lessons.summary: Some problems aren’t yours to solve, and that’s okay.

steps.title: Fixing can overstep
steps.body: Jumping in to fix someone’s problems can feel loving. But some problems belong to them. Trying to solve everything can leave you drained and them less confident.

steps.prompt: Match the urge to fix with a supportive alternative.

pairs.b: Help them plan what to say

pairs.a: Sort out their row with a friend
pairs.b: Listen and ask what they’ll do

steps.why: Supporting someone to handle their own problem helps them grow and keeps you from taking on too much.

steps.prompt: Support without taking over.
words: What do you think you’ll do?
steps.answer: What do you think you’ll do?
steps.why: Asking keeps them in charge of their own problem while you stand alongside them.

steps.prompt: Where do you most want to jump in and fix things?
steps.reply: Noticing that urge lets you choose a gentler kind of support next time.

steps.body: When someone shares a problem this week, ask what they think they’ll do before offering any solutions.

lessons.title: Pause Heavy Talks
lessons.summary: It’s okay to say “Can we pick this up later?”

steps.title: Not every talk needs to happen now
steps.body: Heavy conversations at midnight or when you’re exhausted rarely go well. Asking to pause, and naming when you’ll come back, protects both of you.

steps.prompt: At 11pm, your partner wants to talk about money worries. You’re shattered. What’s best?

options.text: Push through even though you can barely think.
options.why: Tired talks tend to get tense and solve less.

options.text: “This matters, and I’m too tired to do it justice. Breakfast tomorrow?”
options.why: It values the topic, explains why you’re pausing and sets a clear time.

options.text: “Not now.” and roll over.
options.why: A curt brush-off can make them feel their worry doesn’t matter.

steps.prompt: Put a kind pause in order.
steps.why: Showing it matters and offering a real time makes the pause feel caring, not like avoidance.

steps.prompt: When do heavy talks usually happen for you?
steps.reply: If it’s often at a hard time, suggesting a better slot can make those talks go much more smoothly.

steps.body: If a heavy talk starts at a bad time, ask to pause and name a specific time to return to it.

lessons.title: When They Push Back
lessons.summary: People may test a new limit. Stay calm and kind.

steps.title: Pushback is normal
steps.body: When you set a new boundary, people may push, sulk or try to persuade you. That doesn’t mean the boundary is wrong. It often just means it’s new.

steps.title: Testing a new limit

lines.text: Come on, just lend me the car this weekend. You always used to.

steps.prompt: You’ve decided not to lend your car any more. Reply?

options.text: Ugh, fine. Just this once.
options.why: Giving in teaches him that pushing harder works.

options.text: I know I used to, but I’m not lending it any more. Happy to help find a hire car.
options.why: Calm and kind, you held the limit and offered another way to help.

options.text: You’re so selfish for even asking.
options.why: Attacking him turns a clear limit into a fight.

steps.prompt: Holding steady, or giving way?

cards.text: “My answer’s still no, but thanks for understanding.”

steps.why: Calm repetition holds a limit without a fight. Caving or over-explaining tells people the limit can move.

steps.prompt: How do you usually respond to pushback?
steps.reply: Knowing your pattern helps. Calm and kind repetition gets easier with practice.

steps.body: If someone pushes back on a limit this week, repeat it calmly once, without adding new reasons.

lessons.title: Guilt Isn’t a Verdict
lessons.summary: Feeling guilty doesn’t mean you’ve done something wrong.

steps.title: Guilt can be a habit
steps.body: If you’re used to always saying yes, setting a limit can feel guilty, even when it’s fair. That feeling is often just change, not proof you’re being unkind.

steps.prompt: Match the guilty thought to a kinder one.

pairs.b: “They can be upset, and I can be kind.”

steps.why: Kinder thoughts don’t ignore the feeling. They remind you that a fair limit can coexist with care.

steps.prompt: You said no to helping your aunt this weekend and feel guilty. What’s the healthiest step?

options.text: Remind yourself why you said no, and let the feeling pass.
options.why: Guilt fades when you trust your reasons rather than acting on it.

options.text: Call her back and say yes after all.
options.why: Acting on guilt teaches you that limits are only temporary.

options.text: Avoid her for weeks so you don’t feel it.
options.why: Avoiding her keeps the guilt alive and hurts the relationship.

steps.title: When guilt is used against you
steps.body: Some people use guilt to control others. If someone often makes you feel bad for having any limits at all, or you feel afraid, talk to someone you trust or a support service.

steps.prompt: When does guilt hit you hardest?
steps.reply: That’s worth knowing. Next time it hits, try one of those kinder thoughts.

steps.body: When you feel guilty about a limit this week, say a kinder thought to yourself and let the feeling pass.

lessons.title: Repeat, Calmly
lessons.summary: You don’t need new arguments. Just repeat your limit kindly.

steps.title: The broken record
steps.body: When someone keeps pushing, you don’t have to win the debate. Calmly repeating the same kind sentence, like “I understand, and my answer is still no”, is enough.

steps.prompt: Repeat it kindly.
words: and my answer is still no.
steps.answer: and my answer is still no.
steps.why: It acknowledges them and holds your limit, without starting a fresh argument.

steps.prompt: Order a calm repeat when someone pushes.
steps.why: Staying calm and acknowledging them keeps it friendly. Repeating, then moving on, shows the limit isn’t up for debate.

steps.prompt: A salesperson keeps pressing you to sign up today. What works best?

options.text: Explain your whole budget in detail.
options.why: More detail gives them more to argue with.

options.text: “Thanks, I’m not signing up today.” Repeat as needed.
options.why: Short, polite repetition makes your answer clear and final.

options.text: Sign up just to end the conversation.
options.why: Giving in under pressure often leads to regret.

steps.prompt: What’s your go-to calm sentence for holding a limit?
steps.reply: Having one ready makes holding limits much easier in the moment.

steps.body: Choose your own calm repeat sentence and practise saying it out loud a few times today.

lessons.title: It’s Okay to Change
lessons.summary: Your limits can change as your life changes.

steps.title: Limits aren’t carved in stone
steps.body: What felt fine last year might not now. New jobs, babies, health or simply growing can change what you need. Updating a boundary is healthy, not inconsistent.

steps.prompt: You used to host Sunday lunch every week. With a new baby, it’s too much. What’s best?

options.text: Keep hosting so nobody’s disappointed.
options.why: Pushing on when life has changed usually ends in burnout.

options.text: Quietly stop inviting people.
options.why: Stopping without explanation can leave people confused and hurt.

options.text: “With the baby, I can’t host weekly any more. Could we take turns?”
options.why: Honest about the change, and it offers a fair new way to keep the tradition.

steps.prompt: A healthy update, or a reason to feel bad?

cards.text: Needing more sleep since starting a new job
“I should be able to do what I always did.”

steps.why: Life changes, and so do your needs. Updating your limits is a sign of self-awareness, not weakness.

steps.prompt: Which old limit might need updating?
steps.reply: If one stood out, it might be time for a gentle conversation about it.

steps.body: Think of one limit that no longer fits your life. Write down what you’d like it to be now.

lessons.title: Say It Early
lessons.summary: Tell people about a change before it becomes a problem.

steps.title: Early beats explosive
steps.body: If you wait until you’re at breaking point, a changed boundary comes out as a snap. Mentioning it early, while you’re calm, makes it much easier for others to hear.

steps.title: Less time for calls
steps.prompt: Work’s busier and you need shorter calls. Reply?

options.text: Can’t tonight.
options.why: It’s a no without explaining the change, so they may feel brushed off.

options.text: Can’t wait to hear! Work’s busy, so 20 mins tonight and a longer chat on Sunday?
options.why: You shared the change early and kindly, with a plan that still keeps you close.

options.text: Say yes, then get snappy halfway through.
options.why: Waiting until you’re frazzled means the change comes out as irritation.

steps.prompt: Flag the change early.
steps.why: A calm, early heads-up explains the change before it causes any hurt.

steps.prompt: Do you usually mention changes early or late?
steps.reply: Early heads-ups take courage, but they save a lot of hurt later.

steps.body: If a limit of yours has changed, mention it to the people affected this week, while you’re feeling calm.

lessons.title: Update, Don’t Vanish
lessons.summary: Pulling away silently hurts more than an honest update.

steps.title: Ghosting isn’t a boundary
steps.body: Disappearing, ignoring messages or quietly stepping back can feel easier than explaining. But it leaves people confused and hurt. A short, honest update is kinder.

steps.prompt: Honest update, or vanishing act?

cards.text: “I need to step back from the group chat for a bit.”
“I can’t do Fridays any more, but let’s meet up monthly.”
Just not showing up any more

steps.why: A few honest words let people understand the change. Vanishing leaves them to imagine the worst.

steps.prompt: You want to leave a weekly running club that’s become too much. What’s kindest?

options.text: Stop going and stop replying to messages.
options.why: Silence leaves the group wondering if they did something wrong.

options.text: “I’m stepping back from the club for now. Thanks for all the fun runs!”
options.why: Short, honest and warm, it closes things kindly.

options.text: Make up an injury so nobody asks.
options.why: A made-up excuse can be hard to keep up and dents trust if found out.

steps.prompt: Have you ever been ghosted? How did it feel?
steps.reply: Remembering that feeling can help you choose an honest update instead.

steps.body: If you’ve been quietly pulling away from something, send a short, honest update to the people involved.

lessons.title: Ask for Alone Time
lessons.summary: Needing time alone is normal. Ask for it clearly.

steps.title: Everyone needs space
steps.body: Even in close, happy relationships, people need time to themselves. Asking for it clearly, and kindly, stops the other person wondering if something’s wrong.

steps.prompt: You need an evening to yourself, but your partner wants to watch a film together. What’s best?

options.text: “I need a quiet night to recharge. Film tomorrow?”
options.why: Clear, kind and it offers another time, so they don’t feel rejected.

options.text: Watch it but sigh and scroll your phone the whole time.
options.why: Being there unwillingly can feel worse than an honest request for space.

options.text: Go to bed early without saying why.
options.why: Disappearing without a word can leave them worried.

steps.prompt: Ask for space kindly.
steps.before: I love spending time with you,
words: and I need a bit of alone time
steps.answer: and I need a bit of alone time
steps.why: It makes clear the space is about your needs, not about not wanting them.

steps.prompt: How do you recharge best?
steps.reply: Lovely. Knowing what recharges you makes it easier to ask for it.

steps.body: Ask for one small slot of alone time this week, and explain kindly that it helps you recharge.

lessons.title: Space Isn’t Rejection
lessons.summary: When someone needs space, it’s usually not about you.

steps.title: Their space, not your fault
steps.body: When someone asks for time alone, it’s easy to feel rejected. Usually, it’s simply what they need to feel their best, which helps them show up better for you too.

steps.title: They need a quiet weekend

lines.text: Would you mind if I had a quiet weekend at home on my own?

steps.prompt: You’d hoped to see them. What do you say?

options.text: Did I do something wrong?
options.why: Taking it personally can make them feel guilty for having a need.

options.text: Of course. Rest up, and let’s plan something fun next week 💛
options.reaction: Thank you, that means a lot!
options.why: You respected their need and kept warmth and a plan for later.

options.text: Fine, I’ll find someone else to hang out with then.
options.why: Sounding hurt and pointed turns their request into a problem.

steps.prompt: Respects their space, or takes it personally?

cards.text: Texting every hour to check in
Making your own plans for the day

steps.why: Respecting space shows trust and security. Taking it personally puts pressure on them for having a normal need.

steps.prompt: How do you feel when someone close needs space?
steps.reply: All normal feelings. Reminding yourself it’s about their needs, not your worth, can help.

steps.body: The next time someone asks for space, reply warmly and make your own plans for that time.

lessons.title: Come Back as Promised
lessons.summary: Taking space works best when you return when you said.

steps.title: Space with a return date
steps.body: “I need some space” can sound scary if it has no end. Saying when you’ll be back, and keeping to it, makes asking for space feel safe for everyone.

steps.prompt: Put healthy space-taking in order.
steps.why: A clear ask and a return time make space feel safe. Coming back when promised builds trust for next time.

steps.prompt: After an argument, you need time to cool off. What’s the best way to ask?

options.text: Storm out and say nothing.
options.why: Leaving without a word can feel like abandonment in the middle of a row.

options.text: “I need an hour to calm down. Let’s talk again at 8.”
options.why: Clear, time-limited space lets you both calm down and know the talk will continue.

options.text: “I need space” and not return for days.
options.why: Open-ended space can leave the other person anxious and unsure.

steps.prompt: Give your space a time.
steps.before: I need a little time to think.
steps.why: A clear return time reassures them the conversation isn’t over, just paused.

steps.body: Next time you need space, say when you’ll be back, then make sure you return at that time.

lessons.title: Take No Gracefully
lessons.summary: When someone says no to you, thank them and move on.

steps.title: Boundaries go both ways
steps.body: We want people to respect our limits. That means respecting theirs too. Taking a no gracefully shows people it’s safe to be honest with you.

steps.title: A friend says no

lines.text: Fancy coming to my birthday drinks on Saturday? 🎉
I’d love to, but I need a quiet weekend. Sorry!

steps.prompt: How do you reply?

options.text: Totally get it! Let’s do lunch next week instead? 😊
options.why: You took the no warmly and kept the friendship close.

options.text: Seriously? It’s my birthday though…
options.why: Guilt-tripping can push them into a yes they don’t want to give.

options.text: Fine.
options.why: A short, cold reply can feel like punishment for being honest.

steps.prompt: Accept a no kindly.
steps.why: Thanking them for honesty makes it easier for them to be truthful with you again.

steps.prompt: How do you usually feel when someone says no to you?
steps.reply: All fair feelings. You can feel them and still reply kindly.

steps.body: The next time someone says no to you, reply with a warm “No problem, thanks for being honest.”

lessons.title: Don’t Push Twice
lessons.summary: Asking again and again after a no wears down trust.

steps.title: Once is enough
steps.body: Asking someone again after they’ve said no, or trying to talk them round, can make them feel pressured. Respecting their first answer makes them trust you more.

steps.prompt: Respectful, or pushing?

cards.text: “Are you sure? It’ll be really fun!”
Asking their friends to persuade them

steps.why: Respecting a no keeps it safe for people to be honest. Pushing can make them say yes just to avoid conflict.

steps.prompt: Your partner says they don’t want to go to your work do. What’s respectful?

options.text: Keep bringing it up all week until they agree.
options.why: Repeated asking wears them down rather than respecting their choice.

options.text: “Okay, I’ll miss you there, but that’s fine.”
options.why: You share your feeling honestly and accept their answer.

options.text: Tell them everyone will think they’re rude.
options.why: Using guilt or worry to change their mind is a form of pressure.

steps.prompt: Do you ever ask twice after a no?
steps.reply: Noticing it is great. Accepting the first answer is a quiet but powerful kindness.

steps.body: This week, when someone says no, accept their first answer without asking again.

lessons.title: Respect Their Limits
lessons.summary: Their limits may differ from yours, and that’s okay.

steps.title: Different, not wrong
steps.body: Someone might need more sleep, less noise or fewer hugs than you. Their limits don’t have to make sense to you to deserve respect.

steps.prompt: Match their limit to a respectful response.

pairs.b: Suggest a café instead of a pub

steps.why: Small adjustments show you care about their comfort, even when their needs differ from yours.

steps.prompt: Your new friend says they’re not a hugger. What’s the respectful response?

options.text: “Oh, come on, everyone loves a hug!”
options.why: Pushing past a stated limit can make them feel unsafe around you.

options.text: Hug them anyway as a joke.
options.why: Ignoring a physical limit, even jokingly, isn’t okay.

options.text: “No problem! High five instead?”
options.why: You accept their limit warmly and find another friendly way to connect.

steps.prompt: Whose limits do you find hardest to understand?
steps.reply: That’s okay. Respecting a limit doesn’t require fully understanding it.

steps.body: Ask someone close if there’s anything you do that they’d prefer you didn’t, and listen without defending.

lessons.title: Check Your Limits
lessons.summary: A regular check-in shows which limits need attention.

steps.title: Your body keeps score
steps.body: Tiredness, resentment and dread are useful signals. They often point to a limit that’s being crossed. A quick weekly check helps you notice before it builds up.

steps.prompt: Match the feeling to what it might be telling you.

pairs.b: This may be too much now
I gave more than I wanted

steps.why: Feelings like these are clues, not failures. They show where a limit might need setting or updating.

steps.prompt: Put a weekly limits check in order.
steps.why: Reflecting first, then choosing just one thing to change, keeps it gentle and doable.

steps.prompt: What drained you most this week?
steps.reply: That’s a great place to look for a small limit to adjust.

steps.body: At the end of this week, spend five minutes noticing what drained you and choose one limit to adjust.

lessons.title: Boundaries with Kindness
lessons.summary: Limits are about caring for yourself, not shutting people out.

steps.title: Gates, not walls
steps.body: A healthy boundary is like a garden gate: it keeps what matters safe, but still lets people in. Kind limits help relationships last because they stop resentment from growing.

steps.prompt: A kind gate, or a cold wall?

cards.text: “I can’t talk now, but I’d love to later.”
“I need weekends for rest, but weeknights work.”
Cutting people off without a word

steps.why: Kind gates protect you while keeping connection. Cold walls protect you too, but often cost the relationship.

steps.prompt: Your friend often calls during your work hours. What’s a kind gate?

options.text: Block their number during the day.
options.why: Blocking without a word can feel hurtful and confusing.

options.text: Answer every call even when it’s stressful.
options.why: Ignoring your own needs builds quiet resentment.

options.text: “I can’t chat during work, but I’d love a call after 6!”
options.why: It sets the limit and invites them in at a better time.

steps.prompt: Do your boundaries tend to be gates or walls?
steps.reply: Whatever you find, kind gates are always something you can build towards.

steps.body: Turn one “no” this week into a kind gate by adding when or how you can say yes.

lessons.title: Keep Them Up
lessons.summary: Limits need gentle, regular care to keep working.

steps.title: Boundaries need watering
steps.body: Like a garden, boundaries need regular attention. Old habits creep back and life changes. Small, steady care keeps your limits healthy without big confrontations.

steps.prompt: You set a limit on weekend work emails, but you’ve started checking them again. What helps?

options.text: Give up, it’s too hard to keep.
options.why: Slipping is normal. It doesn’t mean the limit was wrong.

options.text: Gently reset it, maybe by turning off notifications.
options.why: A small practical step helps you get back on track without guilt.

options.text: Be strict and harsh with yourself about it.
options.why: Self-criticism rarely helps habits stick; gentle resets work better.

steps.prompt: Reset kindly.
steps.before: I’ve slipped a bit lately, so
steps.why: Kind restarts make it easy to keep going. Slips are part of building any habit.

steps.prompt: What have you learned most about boundaries in these lessons?
steps.reply: Wonderful. Keep tending your limits gently, and they’ll keep looking after you.

steps.body: Choose one limit that’s slipped lately and take one small, practical step to reset it this week.
